item.title: Typhoon Noul disrupts Fiji Airways Hong Kong flights
item.description: Fiji Airways has cancelled its scheduled service from Nadi to Hong Kong as Typhoon Noul continues to disrupt air travel across Hong Kong, with passengers urged to monitor the latest flight updates as the severe weather system approaches. The airline confirmed that Flight FJ393, scheduled to depart Nadi for Hong Kong yesterday, had been cancelled due to the impact of the typhoon.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji Airways has cancelled its scheduled service from Nadi to Hong Kong as Typhoon Noul continues to disrupt air travel across Hong Kong, with passengers urged to monitor the latest flight updates as the severe weather system approaches.

The airline confirmed that Flight FJ393, scheduled to depart Nadi for Hong Kong yesterday, had been cancelled due to the impact of the typhoon.

Fiji Airways says its teams are already in direct contact with all affected passengers and has arranged a supplementary service to minimise disruption.

The replacement FJ393 flight will now depart Nadi at 1:30pm today, while the return FJ392 service from Hong Kong will depart at 9:30pm on 26 July (Hong Kong time).

The national carrier is encouraging customers to regularly check the Fiji Airways website for updated flight information, saying it will continue to monitor the situation closely and make further operational changes if necessary.

“The safety of our passengers and crew remains our highest priority,” Fiji Airways said.

The airline also thanked customers for their patience and understanding as weather conditions continue to affect operations.

Meanwhile, Hong Kong International Airport (HKIA) says Typhoon Noul has already caused significant disruption to flight schedules.

As of 4:50pm on 25 July, airport authorities reported that 29 departing flights and 20 arriving flights had been cancelled, while 126 departures and 112 arrivals had been delayed.

Airport officials have warned that a much larger number of flights are expected to be affected on 26 July as the storm moves closer to Hong Kong.

item.title: Electoral Review Commissioners defend electoral reform recommendations
item.description: The commissioners behind Fiji’s 2025 Electoral Law Reform Commission (FELRC) have defended their proposed electoral reforms, insisting the recommendations are based on what ordinary Fijians told them during months of nationwide consultations rather than abstract theories of proportional representation. item.content:encoded:
The commissioners behind Fiji’s 2025 Electoral Law Reform Commission (FELRC) have defended their proposed electoral reforms, insisting the recommendations are based on what ordinary Fijians told them during months of nationwide consultations rather than abstract theories of proportional representation.

Responding to criticism from Dialogue Fiji Executive Director Nilesh Lal, former Chief Justice Daniel Fatiaki and Professor Wadan Narsey said the commission’s report, An Electoral System for the People From the People , was developed after extensive consultations throughout Fiji and in accordance with its terms of reference.

The commissioners expressed surprise at claims that Fiji’s current electoral system provides a more accurate reflection of voters’ choices than the commission’s proposed Proportional Open List Constituency System (POLCS).

“It is therefore utterly astonishing that the executive director of Dialogue Fiji baldly and abstractly claims ‘Fiji’s current electoral system delivers a more accurate reflection of voters’ choices than the proposed Proportional Open List Constituency System (POLCS) being considered during constitutional reform’,” the commissioners said.

They argued that the focus should be on the concerns repeatedly raised by members of the public rather than mathematical proportionality.

“Instead, the executive director of Dialogue Fiji is fixated upon some hypothetical arithmetical proportionality which the people of Fiji would have little understanding of, or care for, or even, the slightest interest in,” they said.

According to the commissioners, public consultations revealed widespread dissatisfaction with the existing electoral system.

They said voters complained about the “confusing Sudoku style ballot paper” containing hundreds of random numbers, the lack of identifiable local Members of Parliament, the five per cent threshold that excludes candidates with significant support, and excessive powers held by some electoral officials.

Instead, they said Fijians consistently called for local constituencies, accountable MPs, simpler ballot papers displaying candidate names, party symbols and photographs, straightforward voting procedures and transparent counting of ballots.

The commissioners said the proposed POLCS delivers exactly those priorities.

“It needs to be emphasised to Dialogue Fiji that the 2025 POLCS responds first and foremost to what the people and voters of Fiji wanted from their electoral system namely, their own locally accountable MPs,” they said.

Under the proposal, Fiji would have 25 open constituencies and 25 reserved seats for women, creating 50 locally accountable MPs, while 21 list seats would promote proportionality and allow greater representation for smaller parties and independents.

The commissioners also dismissed concerns over the possibility of overhang seats, describing them as unlikely and manageable.

“In any case the Fiji Electoral Commission would first allocate the 21 List MPs to all the other deserving parties who qualify for a share of the national Parliament,” they said, adding that the commission could approve “a small number of ‘overhang’ or ‘compensatory’ seats” if required.

Looking ahead, the commissioners said they expected the Constitution Review Commission’s report to reflect similar recommendations following its own nationwide consultations.

“Given that it has also consulted widely throughout Fiji, we doubt if electoral recommendations be much different from that of the 2025 FELRC, certainly not when it comes to the public’s call for local representation and accountability of MPs.”

item.title: Fiji’s exports to US surge 70.4 percent in May
item.description: Fiji’s domestic exports to the United States rose by 70.4 per cent in May 2026, helping drive growth in the country’s international merchandise trade, according to the Fiji Bureau of Statistics. The latest International Merchandise Trade Statistics show exports to the United States increased by $21.9 million to $52.9 million compared with May 2025.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji’s domestic exports to the United States rose by 70.4 per cent in May 2026, helping drive growth in the country’s international merchandise trade, according to the Fiji Bureau of Statistics.

The latest International Merchandise Trade Statistics show exports to the United States increased by $21.9 million to $52.9 million compared with May 2025.

The increase was driven by higher exports of aircraft and ships’ stores, mineral water and mahogany.

Exports to China also recorded strong growth, rising 72.3 per cent to $17.1 million, largely due to increased shipments of gold ores and concentrates, mineral water and non-coniferous timber products.

Exports to South Africa doubled to $5.2 million, supported by exports of precious metal scrap and unwrought silver.

Meanwhile, exports to New Zealand rose 22 per cent to $8 million, led by electrical conductors, taro and kava.

Australia was the only major export destination to record a decline, with exports falling 17.5 per cent to $20.9 million because of lower shipments of non-monetary gold, stainless steel scrap and leguminous vegetables.

On the import side, Singapore remained Fiji’s largest source of imports, increasing 36.7 per cent to $195.5 million, mainly due to higher imports of diesel, residual fuel oil and alcoholic preparations.

Imports from Malaysia recorded the largest percentage increase, surging 435.9 per cent to $64.7 million, driven by aviation turbine fuel, diesel and light oils.

Imports from China remained relatively stable at $113.7 million, while imports from New Zealand increased 5.9 per cent to $81.9 million and imports from Australia rose 6.3 per cent to $75.1 million.

Fiji’s re-export trade also strengthened, with exports to Tonga more than doubling to $25 million, driven by diesel, aviation turbine fuel and light oils.

Re-exports to the Cook Islands, New Caledonia and Tuvalu also recorded significant increases, reflecting continued demand for fuel products and other goods across the Pacific.

item.title: PM weighs FSC sale
item.description: SELLING the Fiji Sugar Corporation (FSC) to a private company remains an option, Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says. item.content:encoded:
SELLING the Fiji Sugar Corporation (FSC) to a private company remains an option, Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says.

However, Mr Rabuka said FSC was considered a strategic asset and any decision on its future would need to take into account its importance as a public enterprise. “Selling is an option, but there are certain things that we call strategic assets, and these are strategic assets,” he said.

“They belong to the Government, and what we can do is improve the performance of the industry.”

Mr Rabuka made the comments following concerns over the amount of Government funding used to support the sugar industry, including about $18 million annually to pay off FSC’s debt.

Sugar Minister Tomasi Tunabuna had earlier raised concerns about the significant investment required to revive the sugarcane sector and improve the industry’s performance.

Mr Rabuka said the Government was focused on improving the industry’s performance while considering options for its future.

He said the Special Committee on the Sugar Industry was engaging with stakeholders to gather their views on challenges facing the sector.

The committee has already visited sugar-growing areas in the Western Division and is expected to travel to the North for further consultations.

Sugar remains a major industry in Fiji, supporting thousands of farmers and contributing to the economy.

item.title: Union demands fix for teacher pay delays
item.description: THE Fiji Teachers Union (FTU) has called on the Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Finance to urgently address delays in paying newly-appointed teachers, saying no employee should be expected to work without receiving their wages. In a statement, FTU general secretary Muniappa Goundar said the union was deeply concerned that many new teachers across the country had reported for duty and con
item.content:encoded:
THE Fiji Teachers Union (FTU) has called on the Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Finance to urgently address delays in paying newly-appointed teachers, saying no employee should be expected to work without receiving their wages.

In a statement, FTU general secretary Muniappa Goundar said the union was deeply concerned that many new teachers across the country had reported for duty and continued teaching despite not receiving their salaries.

“These teachers have honoured their commitment to the education of Fiji’s children,” Mr Goundar said.

“Yet, fortnight after fortnight, they are met with the same response: ‘Your salary is still being processed.’ The question is: How long must they continue to wait?”

He said teachers faced financial responsibilities from the day they started work, including paying rent, transport, food expenses, loan repayments and supporting their families.

“No employee should be expected to work without being paid for services already rendered.”

Mr Goundar said the Employment Relations Act 2007 recognised the protection of wages and required workers to be paid in a timely manner for work performed.

The union has called on the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Finance and the Education Ministry’s salaries section to treat the matter as a priority.

“Our new teachers deserve respect, dignity and the timely payment of their hard-earned wages.”

item.title: Fuel price hike looms
item.description: FUEL prices are expected to rise again next month due to ongoing international tensions in the Middle East. Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka said the Government had been informed of the expected increase, which was linked to overseas developments.
item.content:encoded:
FUEL prices are expected to rise again next month due to ongoing international tensions in the Middle East.

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka said the Government had been informed of the expected increase, which was linked to overseas developments.

“There has been an increase in the prices of goods. Yesterday we were told that the price of fuel would increase,” he said.

Mr Rabuka said the increase was being driven by international conflicts that had pushed up global fuel prices, which were beyond the Government’s control.

“We thought the increase in fuel prices would stop.”

Mr Rabuka made the comments while speaking at the launch of the Fiji Blue Economy and Green Growth Community Development Program at Koronatoga Village in Cakaudrove yesterday.

He said international events continued to have a direct impact on Fiji’s economy, particularly through higher fuel costs, which also affected the prices of goods and services.

Fuel prices in Fiji are reviewed monthly by the Fijian Competition and Consumer Commission based on changes in international refined fuel prices, freight costs and the exchange rate.

The next fuel price announcement is expected at the end of the month.

item.title: Rabuka defends cost of CoI
item.description: MONEY spent on the Commission of Inquiry was not wasted because ensuring good governance is worth the investment, Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says. Mr Rabuka defended the estimated $2million spent on the Commission of Inquiry (CoI), saying the process was never intended to prosecute anyone but to investigate allegations and establish the facts.
item.content:encoded:
MONEY spent on the Commission of Inquiry was not wasted because ensuring good governance is worth the investment, Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says.

Mr Rabuka defended the estimated $2million spent on the Commission of Inquiry (CoI), saying the process was never intended to prosecute anyone but to investigate allegations and establish the facts.

“It’s not wasted. Any amount of money spent on ensuring good governance is justifiable,” Mr Rabuka said.

Responding to questions on claims that the inquiry had concluded without enough evidence to lay charges, Mr Rabuka said there was a misunderstanding about the role of the commission.

“Well, the Court of Inquiry or the Commission of Inquiry is not a prosecutorial process. They are not there to prosecute,” he said.

“It is inquisitorial. They are doing an inquisition, like investigative. After the investigation, then you put it to those that will progress it to the prosecution level.”

Mr Rabuka said the commission’s responsibility was to establish what had occurred and determine whether any findings pointed to possible breaches of the law.

He said the $5000-a-day payment for CoI commissioner Justice David Ashton-Lewis was part of a deal approved by Cabinet before he was appointed.

Mr Rabuka made the comments when asked if he was aware of the payment made to the retired Australian judge who led the Commission of Inquiry into the appointment of Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption commissioner Barbara Malimali.

He said Cabinet had approved the terms of Justice Ashton-Lewis’ appointment before the inquiry began.

item.title: CJ urges lawyers to maintain ethical standards
item.description: CHIEF Justice Salesi Temo has urged new lawyers to build their reputations through honesty and never to step outside “the four corners of the law” even when pressured by clients. Speaking to 11 newly- admitted lawyers yesterday, Justice Temo said legal practitioners must remain committed to ethical practices while advocating fearlessly for those they represent.
item.content:encoded:
CHIEF Justice Salesi Temo has urged new lawyers to build their reputations through honesty and never to step outside “the four corners of the law” even when pressured by clients.

Speaking to 11 newly- admitted lawyers yesterday, Justice Temo said legal practitioners must remain committed to ethical practices while advocating fearlessly for those they represent.

He said a lawyer’s conduct in the courtroom played a significant role in earning the respect of the bench.

“I’ve come through lawyers who fight fearlessly but are not polite in the courtroom and I’ve come through lawyers who are very polite in the courtroom,” he said.

Justice Temo said, in his view, the most effective lawyers were those who remained courteous.

He said politeness could be a powerful advocacy tool, admitting there had been occasions when he later questioned decisions he had made after being persuaded by courteous counsel.

“You are in the courtroom, you are nothing but an advocate.

“Your clients. You are not there to decide for them. The one who’s going to decide is the one who sits on the bench.”

He said lawyers should focus on persuading the court through professional advocacy while recognising that judges closely observe their conduct.

“For us on the bench, we observe you lawyers as you appear before us. Reputation is what you build in the courtroom.”

Justice Temo said a strong reputation was earned through hard work, honesty and courage, but stressed that lawyers must always operate within the law.

He also cautioned the new lawyers against giving in to pressure from clients to act improperly.

“Some of your clients may try and persuade you to work outside the four corners of the law. Please don’t go that way. Stay within the four corners,” he said.
